question: What is the main weakness of primary radar that SSR overcomes?

options.text: It cannot measure the range of an aircraft
It cannot give the bearing of an aircraft
It cannot be used above FL 245 at all

explanation: Primary radar gives good range and bearing but no positive identity, which ATC needs in busy airspace. It also needs high power for the two-way echo.

question: What equipment does an aircraft need for SSR?
explanation: The ground interrogator sends pulses and the aircraft's transponder replies automatically with coded pulses. Each path is one-way, which needs far less power than an echo.

question: Which is an advantage of SSR over primary radar?

options.text: It needs far less power for the same coverage
It works without any equipment in the aircraft
It gives a more accurate bearing
It shows weather as well as aircraft

explanation: SSR reaches 200–250 NM with low power, ignores the target's size and aspect, is free of clutter, identifies aircraft, shows altitude, speed and track history, and can flag an emergency.

question: Why is an SSR reply free of clutter?

options.text: It uses a lower frequency than primary radar
It is a transmission, not a reflected echo
It is filtered by moving target indication

explanation: The reply comes from the transponder on a different frequency, so ground and weather reflections of the interrogation are never displayed.

question: Why are SSR and primary radar usually co-located?

options.text: Because SSR cannot work at all without the primary radar echoes
To add identity and altitude to accurate position
Because they share the same frequency
To reduce the power of the primary radar

explanation: Primary radar gives the better position; SSR adds identity, altitude, speed and emergency status. The SSR aerial is often mounted on top of the primary aerial.

question: Which information can be shown beside an aircraft's SSR return?

options.text: Departure time and aircraft registration only
Heading, wind and outside air temperature
Fuel remaining, cabin altitude and weight

explanation: The combined display shows callsign or flight number, pressure altitude or flight level, ground speed and destination.

question: On which frequencies does SSR operate?

options.text: Ground interrogates on 962 MHz; aircraft replies on 1 213 MHz
Ground interrogates on 1 090 MHz; aircraft replies on 1 030 MHz
Ground interrogates on 1 030 MHz; aircraft replies on 1 090 MHz

explanation: The interrogator transmits on 1 030 MHz and receives on 1 090 MHz; the transponder does the opposite. Both are in the UHF band.

question: What radiation pattern do the SSR ground and aircraft aerials have?

options.text: Ground: narrow beam; aircraft: all round
Ground: omnidirectional; aircraft: narrow forward beam

explanation: The ground antenna sends a narrow horizontal beam (giving bearing), while the aircraft's aerial radiates all round.

question: What does a Mode A interrogation ask for?
explanation: Mode A is the identification interrogation; Mode C asks for automatic height read-out.

question: How is a Mode A interrogation distinguished from Mode C?

options.text: By the spacing between pulses P1 and P2
By the spacing between pulses P1 and P3
By the frequency of the interrogation
By the strength of the P2 pulse

explanation: P1–P2 is always 2 µs. P1–P3 is 8 µs for Mode A and 21 µs for Mode C.

question: What is the P1 to P3 spacing of a Mode C interrogation?
explanation: 21 µs for Mode C, 8 µs for Mode A. 20.3 µs is the spacing of the reply's framing pulses.

question: How far apart are the two framing pulses of an SSR reply?
explanation: F1 and F2 are 20.3 µs apart, with the information pulses between them, spaced 1.45 µs.

question: How many SSR Mode A codes are available?
explanation: Twelve information pulses, each present or absent, give 2¹² = 4 096 codes. Mode S's 24-bit address gives over 16.7 million.

question: Why do SSR codes never contain the digits 8 or 9?

options.text: 8 and 9 are reserved for military use
The transponder dial has only seven positions
8 and 9 look too similar on the display
Each digit uses three pulses: values 0–7

explanation: Each of the four digits is made from three pulses (values 1, 2 and 4), so it can only be 0 to 7. Codes run from 0000 to 7777.

question: What happens when the pilot presses IDENT?

options.text: The Mode C altitude is sent in 25 ft steps
An SPI pulse is sent for about 20 seconds
The transponder switches to Mode S for 1 minute

explanation: The special position identification pulse follows the last framing pulse for about 20 seconds, making that aircraft's return distinctive when ATC asks the pilot to "squawk ident".

question: What is the X pulse in an SSR reply for?
explanation: The X pulse is reserved for Mode B, which is not used at present.

question: To what pressure datum is Mode C altitude referenced?

options.text: The pressure set on the standby altimeter
The QNH set on the altimeter

explanation: The encoder is driven by the altimeter's capsule, independent of its subscale setting, so Mode C always reports pressure altitude relative to 1013 hPa. The ground system converts it if needed.

question: Up to what altitude can Mode C report?
explanation: Mode C automatic altitude telemetering works up to 128 000 ft.

question: In what increments does the Mode C read-out change?
explanation: The output changes every 100 ft, the change points being at the 50 ft marks. An aircraft at FL 65 shows 065 until it descends below 6 450 ft, when 064 appears.

question: An aircraft at FL 70 shows 070. As it climbs, at what altitude will the read-out change to 071?
explanation: Changes occur at the 50 ft point between hundreds, so 070 changes to 071 at 7 050 ft.

question: What may ATC tell a pilot if Mode C differs from the reported level by more than the tolerance?

options.text: Select 7700 until the error has been corrected on the ground
Climb or descend to match the Mode C read-out

explanation: Under the international standard a difference of more than 300 ft leads to an instruction to switch off Mode C; if that cannot be done separately, code 0000 shows a transponder malfunction.

question: What Mode C verification tolerance is applied in the UK?
explanation: The international standard is 300 ft, but the UK and other countries apply ±200 ft.

question: When reporting level to ATC, to what accuracy should the pilot read the altimeter to help verify Mode C?
explanation: Reading to the nearest 100 ft allows ATC to compare it with the Mode C read-out.

question: When may a pilot change the transponder code or switch it off in flight?

options.text: After each change of flight level

explanation: Codes are selected, reselected or switched off only on ATS instruction. A code already assigned is kept until told otherwise, and code settings are read back.

question: Unless told otherwise, how should Mode C be operated?
explanation: Mode C is selected simultaneously with Mode A unless an ATS unit instructs otherwise, including with the special codes.

question: Which code indicates an emergency?
explanation: 7700 emergency, 7600 radio failure, 7500 unlawful interference, 7000 conspicuity.

question: Which code indicates radio communication failure?
explanation: 7600 tells ATC the aircraft has lost radio communication.

question: Which code indicates unlawful interference (hijack)?
explanation: 7500 indicates unlawful interference, unless circumstances warrant 7700.

question: An aircraft already squawking a discrete code with ATC has an emergency. Must it change to 7700?

options.text: No; 7700 is used only by military aircraft
No; the code may be kept at discretion
Yes; 7700 must always be set at once
Yes; but only after a MAYDAY call

explanation: 7700 should be set as soon as practicable, giving priority to flying the aircraft. If already on a discrete code and receiving a service, that code may be kept.

question: Which code should a UK pilot squawk when not given one by ATC?
explanation: 7000 is the UK conspicuity code, with Mode C, at all levels unless ATS gives another code or a special code applies.

question: What does code 0000 indicate?
explanation: Code 0000 is used to indicate a malfunction when Mode C cannot be switched off on its own.

subtopic: Disadvantages of Modes A and C
question: What is SSR garbling?

options.text: Overlapping replies from aircraft close in line
A transponder replying on the wrong frequency
Reflections of the interrogation from buildings
Interference from replies that were triggered by another interrogator

explanation: Replies from two aircraft on nearly the same bearing and within about 1.7 NM of each other in range overlap and corrupt each other.

subtopic: Disadvantages of Modes A and C
question: Why does garbling occur when aircraft are within about 1.7 NM in range?

options.text: A reply lasts 20.3 µs, about 1.7 radar miles
The ground beam is 1.7 NM wide at all ranges
SSR range accuracy is only 1.7 NM

explanation: 20.3 µs / 12.36 µs per radar mile ≈ 1.64 NM. Replies from aircraft closer together than that overlap.

subtopic: Disadvantages of Modes A and C
question: What is SSR fruiting?

options.text: A loss of replies in heavy rain
A transponder replying to its own transmission
Overlapping replies from two close aircraft

explanation: A transponder answering another station's interrogations sends replies that this interrogator receives too, cluttering its display.

question: What does the S in Mode S stand for?
explanation: Mode S interrogates aircraft selectively by their unique address, while remaining compatible with Modes A and C.

question: How many discrete addresses does Mode S provide?
explanation: A 24-bit address gives 2²⁴ ≈ 16.7 million codes. Each aircraft is given one at manufacture for life.

question: How is a Mode S aircraft address assigned?

options.text: By the pilot on the control panel
Randomly each time the transponder starts

explanation: The 24-bit address is incorporated at manufacture and stays with the aircraft.

question: In what increments can Mode S report altitude?
explanation: Mode S can report altitude in 25 ft increments (with suitable avionics), though controllers still see 100 ft steps.

question: Which Mode S interrogation is sent to all transponders and asks for no reply?
explanation: All Call acquires Mode S transponders; Broadcast gives information to all with no reply; Selective addresses one transponder; Intermode all-call gets replies from A/C and acquires S.

question: What extra pulse does Mode S use?
explanation: A long P4 makes it a Mode A/C/S All Call; a short P4 makes it Mode A/C-only All Call.

question: Which is a benefit of Mode S?

options.text: It works without a ground network
It removes the need for a transponder

explanation: Selective interrogation and better resolution eliminate synchronous garble, resolve over-interrogation, simplify identification with reflections, and relieve code shortage.

question: How will Mode S reduce R/T workload?

options.text: Much routine information goes by data link
It increases the number of VHF channels
Pilots no longer need to talk to ATC at all
It allows two pilots to share a frequency

explanation: Data link carries many messages via the aircraft's CDU, and code verification calls become unnecessary.

question: In Mode S, what is Comm-B?
explanation: Comm-A: standard ground to air. Comm-B: standard air to ground (ground or air initiated). Comm-C: extended uplink. Comm-D: extended downlink.

question: What is the minimum Mode S transponder level for international flights?
explanation: Level 2 adds standard-length data link and automatic aircraft identification reporting. Level 1 has no data link and is not used for international flights.

question: What does a Level 4 Mode S transponder add to Level 3?
explanation: Level 3 adds extended uplink (ground to air); Level 4 adds extended downlink (air to ground).

question: Which is a basic Mode S downlink aircraft parameter (DAP)?
explanation: Basic DAPs: flight identity, transponder capability, altitude in 25 ft steps and flight status. Heading, speed, roll angle, track angle rate, vertical rate and true track/ground speed are enhanced DAPs.

question: Which is an enhanced Mode S downlink parameter?
explanation: Enhanced parameters include magnetic heading, speeds, roll angle, track angle rate, vertical rate and true track/ground speed.

question: Which aircraft intentions are recommended for future Mode S downlink?

options.text: Selected flight level and selected heading

explanation: Downlinking the selected altitude and selected heading is recommended once technical and institutional issues are resolved.
